title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: six intelligences and one draft

questions.prompt: Karim is forty and has just published a first novel that everybody calls astonishing. A journalist writes: "Karim is a prodigy." Why is the sentence wrong?

options.text: because a prodigy is something you have, not somebody you are
because a prodigy is a young person, and Karim is forty
because a prodigy has to be gifted at maths, not at writing
because a prodigy is somebody nobody has ever taught

questions.explanation: "because a prodigy is a young person, and Karim is forty" is the reason: youth is part of the meaning, which is why the word fits a child of eight who passes an O level and not a writer of forty. "because a prodigy is something you have, not somebody you are" reads the word as a gift: a prodigy is somebody you ARE, so the shape of the journalist's sentence is right and only the age is wrong. "because a prodigy is somebody nobody has ever taught" takes the definition of a gift, a natural ability nobody taught you, and hangs it on the wrong word. "because a prodigy has to be gifted at maths, not at writing" invents a limit the word does not carry: the subject changes nothing. Astonishing is not enough: the word also says young.

questions.prompt: Meriem answers yes to the whole set about making and mending things, and yes to the whole set about listening to other people. What does the questionnaire tell her?

options.text: that she must choose which of the two types she really is
that her two sets of answers cancel out and the test failed
that she is more intelligent than a classmate who said yes once
that both types are hers — a pupil can have more than one

questions.explanation: "that both types are hers — a pupil can have more than one" is what the questionnaire says: mending things and listening to people are two different doors, and a pupil often walks through two or three of them. "that she must choose which of the two types she really is" turns a description into a choice nobody asked for. "that her two sets of answers cancel out and the test failed" reads the questionnaire as a machine with one single output, and "that she is more intelligent than a classmate who said yes once" counts how often she said yes instead of sorting what she said — the competition the lesson refuses.

questions.prompt: You have chosen your statements, found your examples, added the age, the appearance and the background, and written a first draft. What does the lesson ask you to do next?

options.text: Correct your own draft yourself and write it out again.
Copy it neatly into your notebook and hand it in.
Exchange it with a partner and read his draft too.
Look for three more gifted people to describe.

questions.explanation: "Exchange it with a partner and read his draft too." is the next move: the draft exists to be read by somebody else, who then suggests improvements on the ideas, the grammar and the vocabulary. "Copy it neatly into your notebook and hand it in." skips that reading altogether. The classic trap is "Correct your own draft yourself and write it out again.": it looks like serious work, but the lesson wants another pair of eyes on the draft before you rewrite it. And "Look for three more gifted people to describe." invents work the lesson never asks for.

questions.prompt: The last line of the text about John Adams says that being gifted is not rare. A pupil concludes: "Then the questionnaire is useless — we are all the same." Which sentence corrects him?

options.text: Every youngster has a gift, but not the same one.
The questionnaire puts the most gifted pupils first.
A gift has to be earned by working hard at school.
A gift is the same thing in every youngster.

questions.explanation: "Every youngster has a gift, but not the same one." is the correction: the text spreads the gift widely, and the questionnaire exists precisely because what changes from one pupil to the next is the KIND of gift, not the fact of having one. "A gift is the same thing in every youngster." simply repeats the mistake instead of correcting it. "The questionnaire puts the most gifted pupils first." turns the six types into a ladder, which the lesson refuses, and "A gift has to be earned by working hard at school." forgets that a gift is natural: nobody taught it to you.

questions.prompt: Rym repairs the school's broken chairs herself, and the younger pupils come to her with their worries because she is warm-hearted and listens to them without judging. Which two intelligences does she show?

options.text: artistic and social
emotional and artistic
mechanical and physical
mechanical and social

questions.explanation: "mechanical and social" is the pair: repairing a broken object is the mechanical sign, and listening to what others feel is the social one. "mechanical and physical" would need sport or energy, which nothing in the sentence gives. "artistic and social" and "emotional and artistic" both bring in words or pictures, and Rym neither draws nor writes here. Social and not emotional: the lesson keeps warm-hearted and listening well for social intelligence, while emotional intelligence is getting along with people, influencing their choices and being respected. Read each half of the sentence and give it its own type.

questions.prompt: Nour writes this acrostic: "Playing in the school yard / Understanding new lessons / Painting in the art room / I like reading books / Learning new words / Singing in the big choir." One line breaks the rule of the poem. Which one is it?

options.text: I like reading books
Playing in the school yard
Singing in the big choir
Understanding new lessons

questions.explanation: "I like reading books" is the faulty line: every line of an acrostic opens with a verb in the -ing form, and this one opens with a subject followed by a conjugated verb. Its first letter is right, which is what makes it hard to see: the six initials still spell PUPILS. The trap is the word reading, an -ing form that arrives too late in the line to save it. The five other lines of Nour's poem all begin with their -ing verb.
